what_it_does: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) process data whose structure is a graph — nodes connected by edges — which makes memory access patterns highly irregular and hard to optimize. Processing-in-Memory (PIM) is a technique where small compute units are placed directly inside the memory chip itself, eliminating the slow bus trip data would otherwise take to reach the processor. The catch is that PIM units can only efficiently operate on data stored in their own local bank (section) of memory; data sitting in another bank must travel across chip wires, which is slow. This paper finds that on average only about a third of the data accessed during GNN inference stays local, so most computation still pays a travel penalty. The Anchor architecture tackles this with a two-pronged approach: a software algorithm that partitions the graph so related nodes and edges land in the same memory bank together (minimizing the need for cross-bank trips), paired with a hardware data-flow design that ensures any data that must travel between banks does so exactly once rather than being fetched repeatedly.
